text: Breakneck means dangerously fast, fast enough to break your neck. The Economist says fast growth is common in Silicon Valley, but Anthropic's is something else.
To eke out something is to get it barely or with great effort. Anthropic made an operating profit of just under $1bn, but only after losing $1.7bn the quarter before.
A mainstay is a dependable, long-established part of something. McDonald's is a corporate mainstay, and Anthropic's revenue has now passed it.
Revenue is the total money a company takes in from selling its products, before any costs are subtracted. Anthropic's quarterly revenue rose from $376m to $11.6bn.
A prospectus is the document a company must publish before selling shares to the public, laying out its finances and risks. The Economist mines Anthropic's for warnings.
IPO stands for initial public offering, the first time a company sells its shares to ordinary investors on a stock exchange. Anthropic's is a few weeks away and may be among the largest ever.
An initial public offering, or IPO, is when a private company first sells shares to the public. It raises money and lets early backers cash out some of their stake.
A darling is someone or something that is especially loved or favored. Calling Anthropic the darling of the AI revolution means investors and the press adore it.
Lurking means hiding quietly, ready to appear. Here the warnings are tucked inside the long filing, easy to miss until someone reads closely.
In tech, an AI lab is a company whose main work is researching and building artificial-intelligence models. Anthropic and OpenAI are two of the best-known.
To pull in money means to earn it. Anthropic pulled in $376m of revenue in one quarter, then far more later.
Profitability means making more money than you spend. Unlike many startups, Anthropic has already reached it.
Operating profit is what is left from sales after paying the everyday costs of running the business, such as staff and computing power. It ignores things like taxes and interest.
Computing power is the processing capacity of chips and servers. Training and running AI models needs enormous amounts, and it is scarce and costly.
Efficient means getting more done with less waste. Anthropic says better AI models let it spend a smaller share of sales on computing power.
Caution means being careful about risks. The Economist says a close look at the filing suggests investors should be careful.
Cashflow is the cash actually moving in and out of a business. Free cashflow is what is left after paying for the equipment the business needs. Buying chips directly will eat much of Anthropic's.
A valuation is an estimate of how much a company is worth. Some earlier investors hoped for $2trn, but slower growth might lower the number.
Disappointed means let down because things turned out worse than hoped. Investors expecting a $2trn value may be.
Scorching means burning hot. Applied to growth, it means extremely fast, which is why Anthropic became a target for rivals.

t: put a target on its back
forms: has put a target on its back
text: To put a target on someone's back means to make them the thing rivals aim at. Anthropic's rapid growth drew competitors and customers who built alternatives.
An arch-rival is a main, bitter competitor. OpenAI is Anthropic's, and its coding tool Codex is gaining ground.
Codex is OpenAI's AI tool for writing computer code, a direct competitor to Anthropic's Claude Code.
Claude Code is Anthropic's AI programming tool, a hit product that helped drive its rapid growth.
A craze is a short-lived burst of enthusiasm for something. The article calls 'tokenmaxxing' a short-lived one.

Tokens are the small chunks of text an AI model reads and writes, and usage is billed by them. Tokenmaxxing was a craze of using as many as possible, which companies then began to limit because of the cost.
To impose limits is to set rules that cap something. Companies are doing this with how much their engineers can spend on AI.
Shareholders are the people or firms who own shares of a company, and so own a piece of it.
To warn means to tell someone about a danger ahead. The prospectus warns that growth could slow faster than expected, which companies are required to disclose honestly.
Margins are the share of sales a company keeps as profit after costs. Paying more for computing power squeezes margins.
In AI, compute is short for computing power. Short-term compute means renting it on brief, flexible terms, which usually costs more.
A cloud business rents out computing power and software over the internet. Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft run big ones that also sell Anthropic's products to their customers.
Distribution is how a product gets to buyers. Anthropic increasingly depends on partners for it and pays them for the help.
Nvidia is the company that makes the most sought-after chips for training and running AI.
SpaceX is the rocket and space company. Anthropic has agreed to pay it about $3.1bn a month for access to Nvidia chips.
To back out of a deal is to withdraw from it. Anthropic can leave the SpaceX arrangement with 90 days' notice.
Broadcom is a chip company that designs custom chips for large customers.
Silicon is the material chips are made from, so custom silicon means chips designed for one customer's special needs rather than sold off the shelf.
A capital-intensive business has to spend huge sums on equipment or buildings to operate. Buying chips and data centres makes Anthropic more so.
A data centre is a large building full of computers that store and process data. AI models run in them.
Infrastructure means the basic physical systems something depends on. For AI, that means chips, power and data centres.
Irresponsibly means in a careless way that ignores risk. Anthropic's founders admit its plans may seem so at first glance.
Exponential growth keeps multiplying: each step is bigger than the last, like doubling again and again. The founders argue that AI is on this path.
A trajectory is the path something follows over time. The founders say AI's upward trajectory justifies the big spending.
The founders pledge to take big risks without losing their good sense. The Economist doubts that balance will be easy.
Mind-bending describes something so strange or complex it is hard to wrap your head around.
